title_en: Yang Qingjian v. Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi — dispute over return of betrothal gifts
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over betrothal property; Second instance; Intermediate People's Court; Fujian Province; Taiwan Province; Natural person; Marriage Law; Supreme People's Court Opinions on Cohabitation without Marriage Registration; Determination of nature of betrothal gift; Validity of conditional gift; Return of property after dissolution of engagement; Partial support; Cross-strait marriage; No marriage registration; Cohabitation relationship; Large betrothal gift; Marriage; Zhou Wenpi's dispute over return of betrothal gift
full_text_en:
Yang Qingjian v. Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi — dispute over return of betrothal gift

Plaintiff (counterclaim defendant): Yang Qingjian, male, 41 years old, residing at Wanda Road, Taipei City, Taiwan Province.

Defendant (counterclaim plaintiff): Zhou Baomei, female, 27 years old, residing in Jimei District, Xiamen City, Fujian Province.

Defendant (counterclaim plaintiff): Zhou Wenpi, male, 49 years old, father of defendant Zhou Baomei, residing in Jimei District, Xiamen City, Fujian Province.

Plaintiff Yang Qingjian filed a lawsuit with the Jimei District People's Court of Xiamen, Fujian Province, against defendants Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi over a dispute concerning the return of a betrothal gift.

The plaintiff alleged: After the defendants Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi accepted a betrothal gift of RMB 230,000 from the plaintiff, Zhou Baomei was unwilling to marry the plaintiff and also refused to return the betrothal gift. He requested the court to order the two defendants to return the betrothal gift, return one Xianfeng brand motorcycle that the plaintiff had stored at their home, and bear the litigation costs of this case.

The two defendants answered and filed a counterclaim, alleging: The betrothal gift and the motorcycle were both given by plaintiff Yang Qingjian to defendant Zhou Baomei for the purpose of marriage. The betrothal gift had already been spent on items such as hosting the wedding ceremony, giving red envelopes to the matchmaker, and purchasing new household items, totaling over RMB 174,000. Zhou Baomei and Yang Qingjian had lived together for two months, and their relationship was good. It was only because members of Yang Qingjian's family repeatedly broke their promises and refused for various reasons to allow Yang Qingjian and Zhou Baomei to go through the marriage registration procedures that a dispute arose. This constituted a breach of contract by the plaintiff. The defendants not only had no obligation to return the betrothal gift, but also had the right to demand that the plaintiff compensate Zhou Baomei for her loss of youth and reputation, and make arrangements for Zhou Baomei's future life. They requested the court to order the plaintiff to pay RMB 200,000 as compensation for loss of youth and reputation.

Yang Qingjian replied to the counterclaim, arguing: The counterclaim requests of Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi have no legal basis and should be dismissed.

The Jimei District People's Court of Xiamen found the following facts upon trial:

In August 1998, plaintiff Yang Qingjian and defendant Zhou Baomei became acquainted through the introduction of two matchmakers. Subsequently, with the consent of both parties' parents, they decided to get married. On September 24, Yang Qingjian gave Zhou Baomei a betrothal gift of RMB 230,000. After receiving the money, Zhou Baomei and defendant Zhou Wenpi wrote a receipt stating: "It is hereby acknowledged that I, Zhou Baomei, am marrying Mr. Yang Qingjian of Taiwan on September 24, 1998, and have received from him a betrothal gift of RMB 230,000 exactly for the marriage. If there is any regret, I am willing to return the full amount. Lest words be insufficient as evidence, this receipt is hereby issued. Payees: Zhou Wenpi, Zhou Baomei." At noon that day, the woman's side funded an engagement banquet, and a "wedding ceremony" was held on the same day. In the evening, the two stayed in a hotel. After September 26, Zhou Baomei followed Yang Qingjian to Shanghai and lived together in Yang Qingjian's villa in the name of husband and wife. Yang Qingjian's father, Yang Qingshun, also addressed Zhou Baomei as daughter-in-law. During this period, Yang Qingjian sent his own Xianfeng 90 motorcycle to Zhou Baomei's home, without clarifying at the time whether it was a gift or for storage. On November 24, Zhou Baomei returned to Xiamen after a dispute with members of Yang Qingjian's family. Later, the parties negotiated to dissolve the engagement. Yang Qingjian repeatedly requested Zhou Baomei to return the betrothal gift but failed, and thus filed the lawsuit.

During the trial, plaintiff Yang Qingjian stated: Considering the expenses incurred by defendants Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi for the "wedding ceremony," he agreed to accept a return of RMB 150,000 of the betrothal gift, but the motorcycle must be returned. Zhou Baomei only agreed to return RMB 20,000.

Both parties had no objection to the above facts as found by the court.

The Jimei District People's Court of Xiamen held:

This case is a cross-strait marriage dispute triggered by a huge betrothal gift. The focus of the dispute is to determine the nature of the RMB 230,000 betrothal gift and the motorcycle, and whether they should be returned. To properly resolve this dispute, it is necessary not only to follow legal provisions but also to take into account the actual circumstances of both parties.

In this case, plaintiff Yang Qingjian has resided in Taipei City, Taiwan Province, for many years, while defendants Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi live in a rural area of Fujian Province. Although both parties are Chinese citizens, they come from different legal jurisdictions. This fact has led to differing understandings of engagement and marriage between the parties, giving rise to the present dispute.

Betrothal marriage was once popular in China's history, with betrothal gifts and presents being necessary conditions for marriage under this system. Betrothal marriage treats the woman as a commodity for sale, is usually forced and arranged by parents, deprives the woman of her autonomy in marriage, and is a disguised form of mercenary marriage that should be prohibited. Currently, although betrothal marriage is not recognized by law, it still exists as a folk custom in rural areas of Fujian Province and in Taiwan Province.

Article 7 of the Marriage Law stipulates: "Both the man and the woman who intend to marry must personally go to the marriage registration authority for marriage registration. Those who meet the requirements of this Law shall be registered and issued marriage certificates. Once marriage certificates are obtained, the husband-wife relationship is established." Thus, a marriage can only be established after going through the marriage registration procedures. In this case, the parties did not undergo marriage registration, and there is no marriage between them. Article 3 of the "Several Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on the Handling of Cases of Cohabitation in the Name of Husband and Wife Without Marriage Registration" (hereinafter referred to as the "Several Opinions") provides: "As of the date of implementation of the new Regulations on Marriage Registration Administration by the Ministry of Civil Affairs, cohabitation in the name of husband and wife without marriage registration shall be treated as an illegal cohabitation relationship." Plaintiff Yang Qingjian and defendant Zhou Baomei lived together in the name of husband and wife without registering their marriage; this should be recognized as a cohabitation relationship. Such a relationship is not protected by law and should be dissolved according to law.

Although the Marriage Law does not prohibit the act of entering into an engagement between a man and a woman on their own, it does not recognize the engagement as having legally binding force. The civil law of the Taiwan region of China considers an engagement to have legal effect, but it cannot be enforced by compulsory performance. Plaintiff Yang Qingjian, who came from Taiwan, met defendant Zhou Baomei through an introduction. After both parties and their parents agreed, they entered into an engagement, and Yang Qingjian voluntarily gave a huge betrothal gift to the other party. Yang Qingjian did not give the betrothal gift to force the woman into marriage, nor did Zhou Baomei's side force or arrange the marriage for the purpose of accepting the betrothal gift. The betrothal gift in this case is not a bride price in a mercenary marriage and cannot be dealt with by confiscation.

Article 10 of the Several Opinions provides: "When dissolving an illegal cohabitation relationship, income acquired jointly by both parties during the cohabitation period and property purchased jointly shall be treated as general jointly owned property. Property voluntarily given by one party as a gift to the other party before cohabitation may be handled by reference to the rules on gifts." The betrothal gift was voluntarily given by plaintiff Yang Qingjian to defendant Zhou Baomei's side. However, from the time the parties met to the time they began cohabitation, the period was less than one month, and there was no deep emotional foundation. It cannot be justified that the RMB 230,000 betrothal gift was a gratuitous gift from Yang Qingjian. The giving and accepting of the betrothal gift were based on a precondition, that is, the marriage must be concluded. This intention is clearly expressed in the receipt written by Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi. Accordingly, it can be determined that the huge betrothal gift in this case is a conditional gift.

A conditional gift only becomes effective when the condition is fulfilled. If the condition is not fulfilled, the gift does not have legal effect, and the gift should be returned. In this case, the parties did not register their marriage, and there is no marital relationship between them. The condition attached to the gift was not fulfilled. Defendants Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi should return the betrothal gift to plaintiff Yang Qingjian. Considering that part of the betrothal gift given by Yang Qingjian was already spent on the engagement and "wedding" activities jointly agreed upon by both parties, and that Yang Qingjian also cohabited with Zhou Baomei for a period, the amount to be returned should be weighed based on the above circumstances and the respective living standards of the parties. The claim by Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi that over RMB 174,000 of the betrothal gift was spent on such items as hosting the "wedding ceremony", giving red envelopes to the matchmaker, and purchasing "newlywed" items, is unsubstantiated as they failed to provide evidence and is not upheld. Yang Qingjian expressed during the trial that he only agreed to a return of RMB 150,000 of the betrothal gift, which is an exercise of his own rights. This exercise does not violate legal provisions and should be permitted.

From a legal perspective, there is no marital relationship between the parties. Entering into an engagement is not a civil juristic act, so the law also does not provide for compensation after the dissolution of an engagement. The engagement in this case was voluntarily entered into by both parties and was also voluntarily dissolved by them through negotiation. Entering into the engagement did not cause any loss of reputation to defendant Zhou Baomei. The counterclaim by Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi, alleging that plaintiff Yang Qingjian breached the contract and requesting compensation for Zhou Baomei's loss of youth and reputation, lacks legal basis and should be dismissed.

Defendants Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi admitted that plaintiff Yang Qingjian's Xianfeng 90 motorcycle was stored at their home, but they failed to prove that the motorcycle was voluntarily given by Yang Qingjian as a gift. Yang Qingjian now requests its return; Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi should return it.

In summary, the Jimei District People's Court of Xiamen rendered the following judgment:

1. Defendants Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi shall, within one month from the effective date of this judgment, return to plaintiff Yang Qingjian a betrothal gift of RMB 150,000 and one Xianfeng 90 motorcycle.
2. The counterclaim requests of Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi are dismissed.

After the judgment was announced, Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi, dissatisfied, appealed to the Xiamen Intermediate People's Court. Their grounds were: The betrothal gift was a gratuitous gift from the appellee to the appellants. The court of first instance acknowledged that the betrothal gift was a gift but then characterized it as a conditional civil juristic act, which is inconsistent with the facts of this case and seriously violates the provisions of the Supreme People's Court's judicial interpretations. The court of second instance should reverse and rule that the appellants are not liable to return the betrothal gift.

The Xiamen Intermediate People's Court found upon trial: Appellee Yang Qingjian gave RMB 230,000 as a betrothal gift to Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi for the purpose of marrying appellant Zhou Baomei. The parties did not undergo marriage registration but instead performed a ceremonial "wedding" according to folk customs and then lived together in the name of husband and wife. This "marriage," not recognized by law, constitutes a cohabitation relationship and should be dissolved. Although Yang Qingjian's act of giving the betrothal gift before cohabitation constituted a gift, that gift was aimed at achieving marriage. Since the marriage cannot be realized, the property given for the purpose of marriage should be returned. The court of first instance, based on the actual circumstances of this case, after deducting the expenses incurred for holding the "wedding" ceremony, properly ordered Zhou Baomei and Zhou Wenpi to return the remaining portion of the betrothal gift to Yang Qingjian. The appellants' argument that the RMB 230,000 betrothal gift was a gratuitous gift from Yang Qingjian and should not be returned lacks legal basis and is not adopted. Accordingly, the Xiamen Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on April 17, 2000:

Appeal dismissed, and the original judgment affirmed.
